title: SEO and GEO for .NET content creators
seoTitle: SEO and GEO for .NET content creators: a practical guide
description: How .NET bloggers, YouTubers and newsletter writers can publish content that ranks in search and gets cited in AI answers, based on current guidance.
intro: The content that wins in both Google and AI answers is the same content: original, specific, technically correct work that a developer could not get from a summary. This guide is for anyone publishing about C# and .NET, from bloggers and YouTubers to newsletter writers, speakers and library maintainers.

sections.title: SEO and GEO in one minute

ul: **SEO** (search engine optimization): being found and ranked in classic search results.

**GEO** (generative engine optimization): being retrieved, quoted and cited when someone asks ChatGPT, Copilot, Perplexity, Claude or Google AI Mode a question. The term comes from a [2023 Princeton paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.09735).

blocks.p: The two overlap almost completely. Google describes optimizing for generative AI search as ["still SEO"](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/ai-optimization-guide), and AI assistants mostly retrieve pages through search indexes, so a page that is not indexed and worth ranking rarely gets cited. The extra GEO work is about making your best claims easy to lift and attribute.

sections.title: Write what only you can write

blocks.p: Google's guidance calls the content to avoid "commodity content": generic material any model could produce, like a list of tips that restates what is already online. It contrasts that with first-hand pieces drawn from real experience ([Google, AI optimization guide](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/ai-optimization-guide)). For .NET creators, the difference usually looks like this:

head: Commodity (skip or rethink)
Non-commodity (worth publishing)
rows: "10 EF Core performance tips"
"How we cut a report query from seconds to milliseconds in EF Core: the profile, the fix, the trade-off"
"What is .NET Aspire?"
"Migrating a six-service app to Aspire: what broke and what we kept"
"Minimal APIs vs controllers"
"Benchmarks on our API with BenchmarkDotNet, and why we still use controllers for some endpoints"
A rewrite of the release notes
The release notes tested on a real project, with the breaking change you hit

blocks.p: Practical rules:

ul: **Show the evidence.** Benchmarks with the BenchmarkDotNet output, a runnable repo, screenshots of the profiler, the exact error text.

**Say who you are and how you made it.** Google's "Who, How, Why" asks for a clear byline, an explanation of the process (including any AI use readers would wonder about) and a reason to exist beyond search traffic ([Google, helpful content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content)).

**Use AI as an assistant, not the author.** AI use is not disqualifying in itself, but mass-produced text with little oversight is low effort, and using it mainly to manipulate rankings breaks Google's spam policies.
**Never invent experience.** If you did not run it in production, say "in a sample app".

sections.title: Pick topics developers actually search and ask

blocks.p: Developers search with precise, problem-shaped queries, and AI assistants expand each question into several related searches (Google calls this "query fan-out"). A post that fully solves one real problem tends to match many of those sub-queries without chasing each phrasing.
Query types that work well for .NET content:

ul: **Error messages and exceptions:** the exact text, such as an EF Core migration error or a `System.InvalidOperationException` message. Put it verbatim in the post.
**Version-specific how-tos:** "in .NET 10", "EF Core 11", "C# 14". Versions are a strong signal of freshness and relevance.
**Migrations and upgrades:** .NET Framework to .NET, Newtonsoft.Json to System.Text.Json, Swashbuckle to the built-in OpenAPI support.
**Comparisons and decisions:** "X vs Y for Z", with a clear recommendation and the conditions under which it flips.
**Integration recipes:** a .NET app plus a specific service, such as an MCP server in C# or Aspire with PostgreSQL.

blocks.p: Where to find the real questions:

ul: Questions in your own comments, DMs and newsletter replies.
GitHub issues and discussions on the repos you cover (dotnet/runtime, dotnet/aspnetcore, dotnet/efcore).
Google Search Console queries for posts you already have (see [Measure what is working](#measure)).
"People also ask" boxes and the follow-up questions AI assistants suggest after answering your topic.

blocks.p: **One topic, one page.** Google calls creating a page for every fan-out query an ineffective long-term strategy, so write one strong page per problem rather than many near-duplicates.

sections.title: Structure each post so readers and machines can use it

blocks.p: Google's advice is to organize for humans: clear paragraphs, logical sections and descriptive headings. You do not need to "chunk" content, because Google can find the relevant part of a long page. The structure below is simply good technical writing that also happens to be easy to quote.

ol: **Title that names the problem and the version.** "Fixing slow startup in ASP.NET Core 10 with ReadyToRun" beats "Make your app fly".
**Answer in the first two or three sentences.** State the fix or conclusion, then explain. A reader skimming, and a model extracting, both get the point immediately.
**State the context up front.** .NET version, package versions, OS or hosting, and the date you tested. Example: "Tested on .NET 10, EF Core 10, SQL Server 2022, November 2026."
**Descriptive headings.** Write them as the questions or steps they answer ("Why the query is slow", "Adding a compiled query").

**Real code in code blocks, never screenshots.** Text code can be indexed, copied and quoted; use language tags (`csharp`, `json`, `bash`). Keep samples complete enough to compile, and link the full repo.
**Name things precisely.** Use exact type, package and API names (`IHostedService`, `Microsoft.Extensions.AI`), and link to Microsoft Learn or the GitHub source the first time.
**Back claims with numbers and sources.** Benchmark tables, measured timings, links to the issue or docs.
**End with limits and next steps.** When not to use the approach, known issues, related posts of yours.

blocks.p: For video, the same ideas apply: a specific title, a description that states the answer and versions, chapters, and an accurate transcript. Google recommends supporting text with relevant images and video, following its normal image and video SEO guidance.

The one hard gate for Google's AI Overviews and AI Mode is that a page is indexed and eligible to show with a snippet; there are no additional requirements ([Google, AI features](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features)). Most creator sites fail on basics, not on AI tricks.

head: Area
What to do
Why
rows: Crawling
Allow Googlebot and Bingbot in robots.txt, and check that your CDN or host is not blocking them
Google lists crawl access, including CDN and hosting, as a best practice
ChatGPT search
Allow `OAI-SearchBot`. You can block `GPTBot` (training) separately
Sites that opt out of OAI-SearchBot are not shown in ChatGPT search answers ([OpenAI](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/bots))
Rendering
Serve the article text in the HTML, not only after client-side JavaScript
Google asks for important content to be available as text, and not every crawler renders JavaScript reliably
Titles and descriptions
A unique title (problem plus version) and a meta description that states the answer
Shown in search results and in AI citations
Canonical URL
One canonical URL per post on your own domain
Consolidates signals when the post is reachable at several URLs
Dates and author
Visible published and updated dates, and a byline linking to an about page
Supports the Who, How, Why trust signals
Structured data
`BlogPosting` or `Article` JSON-LD with `author`, `datePublished` and `dateModified`, matching the visible page
Optional for AI features, but helps Google show title, image and date ([Google, Article](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/data-types/article))
Internal links
Link related posts and series to each other
Google lists internal links as a way to make content findable
Performance
Fast, mobile-friendly pages and compressed images
Page experience is on Google's best-practice list

blocks.p: **What you can skip for Google:** llms.txt files, special AI markup and "AI-friendly" rewrites. Google says it does not use llms.txt; creating one neither helps nor hurts Search. Other tools may read it, so add one only if it is cheap for you.

**Do not update dates without updating content.** Changing dates to look fresh is on Google's list of search-engine-first warning signs. Update `dateModified` when you actually retest or revise, and say what changed.

sections.title: Make your work easy for AI answers to cite

blocks.p: AI assistants search, retrieve a handful of pages, and quote the passages that best support their answer. Your job is to be retrievable (the sections above) and then to be the most quotable, trustworthy source among the pages retrieved.
What the evidence says:

ul: In the original [GEO study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.09735) (Aggarwal et al., KDD 2024), adding citations, quotations from relevant sources and statistics boosted a page's visibility in generative engine responses by over 40% across their benchmark. Keyword stuffing did not help. The study used test engines, so treat the numbers as direction, not a guarantee.

Google says content that people find unique, compelling and useful will likely matter more for AI search presence in the long run than any other suggestion in its guide, and that seeking inauthentic "mentions" does not help much ([Google](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/ai-optimization-guide)).

blocks.p: How to apply it to .NET content:

ul: **Write self-contained key sentences.** "In .NET 10, X is enabled by default, so you no longer need Y" can be quoted alone. "As mentioned above, this is now the default" cannot.
**Put numbers next to claims.** Measured allocations, request rates and build times, with the setup that produced them.
**Cite primary sources.** Link the Microsoft Learn page, the GitHub PR or issue, the release notes or the spec, not another blog's summary.

**Be consistent about who you are.** Same name, photo and bio across your site, GitHub, LinkedIn, YouTube and conference pages, with links between them, so assistants can connect the work to one author.
**Publish the code.** A public GitHub repo with a clear README is itself a retrievable, citable source, and it backs up the post.
**Check what assistants say.** Ask ChatGPT, Copilot, Perplexity and Google AI Mode the questions your post answers. Note who they cite and what your post is missing compared with those sources.

sections.title: Publish on your own domain first, then distribute

blocks.p: Your own site is the asset that builds over time; platforms are for reach. Publish the full post on your domain, then adapt it for each channel.

head: Channel
How to cross-post
Notes
rows: DEV Community
Set `canonical_url` in the front matter (or post settings) to your original URL
Supported directly by DEV ([DEV help](https://dev.to/help/writing-editing-scheduling))
Medium
Use "Import a story" with your URL; pasting text manually does not set the canonical
Check formatting and code blocks after import
Hashnode
Set the original article URL in post settings
Same idea as DEV
LinkedIn, X, Bluesky, Threads
Share a native summary with the key finding, then link to the full post
Readers get the point without clicking, and the curious ones click
YouTube
Link the written post and repo in the description; reuse the same title wording and versions
Add chapters and check the transcript for correct API names
Newsletters
Link back to the original rather than pasting the whole post
Lets the original collect the signals

blocks.p: A caveat on canonicals: Google treats `rel=canonical` as a hint, and its documentation says it is not recommended for avoiding duplication by syndication partners; the most effective option is for the partner to block indexing of the copy ([Google, canonical guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/canonicalization-troubleshooting)). For community sites you do not control, give your own domain a head start of a few days before cross-posting.
Being featured by others also helps: guest posts, conference talks, podcast appearances and newsletter features are genuine, earned mentions that assistants and search engines can find.
Check once a month; weekly is noise for most creators.

head: Tool
What it shows
Use it to
rows: [Google Search Console](https://search.google.com/search-console)
Queries, impressions, clicks and indexing. AI Overviews and AI Mode traffic is included in the Performance report under "Web"
Find queries where you rank 5 to 15 and improve those posts; fix indexing errors
[Bing Webmaster Tools](https://www.bing.com/webmasters)
Search data, plus an AI Performance report (public preview since February 2026) with Copilot and Bing AI citations, cited pages and grounding queries
See which posts Copilot cites and for which questions
Google Analytics or similar
Referrals from chatgpt.com, perplexity.ai, copilot.microsoft.com and others
Track AI referral traffic and what those visitors read next
Manual prompt checks
What assistants answer and cite for your topics
Spot gaps against the sources they prefer

blocks.p: Pick a few outcome measures that fit your goal, such as newsletter sign-ups, GitHub stars or returning readers, instead of chasing raw pageviews. AI answers can reduce clicks even when they cite you, so citations and sign-ups are often the better signal.

ul: **AI-written posts published as-is.** Fluent but generic text is exactly the commodity content that neither Google nor AI assistants need, and it often gets .NET details wrong (old APIs, invented methods, mixed versions).
**Rewriting release notes or other blogs.** Link to them and add what you found by trying it.
**Keyword stuffing and "for AI" rewrites.** They did nothing in the GEO study, and Google says its systems understand synonyms.
**Publishing on everything.** Covering many unrelated topics hoping some rank is a Google warning sign. Stay close to what you work with.
**Stale versions without a note.** If a post targets .NET 8 and the advice changed in .NET 10, update it or add a dated note at the top.
**Fake freshness.** Changing the date without changing the content.
**Manufactured mentions.** Paid link lists, comment spam and self-promotional answers on forums.
**Code as images.** It cannot be searched, copied or quoted.

checklist: The post contains something I tested, measured or built myself
Title names the problem and the .NET or package version
The answer or conclusion is in the first two or three sentences
Versions, environment and test date are stated near the top
Headings describe what each section answers
Code is text in tagged code blocks, and the full sample is on GitHub
Key claims carry a number and a link to a primary source
Exact error messages and API names appear verbatim
Byline, published date and updated date are visible
Unique title tag, meta description and canonical URL are set
The article text is in the HTML without JavaScript
robots.txt and the CDN allow Googlebot, Bingbot and OAI-SearchBot
Linked from at least one related post of mine
Cross-posts set a canonical to the original and go out a few days later
Any significant AI help is disclosed where readers would wonder
